disaffect.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English affect English disaffect From dis- + affect.

d.g: To deforest.
To change the status of land from that of a forest to ordinary land.

disafforest.e: From Middle English disafforeten, from Anglo-Norman disaforester and its probable etymon Latin disafforestō. By surface analysis, dis- + afforest.

d.g: To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.
d.x: John disagreed with Mary frequently.

d.g: To fail to conform or correspond with.
d.x: My results in the laboratory consistently disagree with yours.

disagree.e: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.

d.g: To refuse to allow.
d.x: The prisoners were disallowed to contact with a lawyer.

d.g: To reject as invalid, untrue, or improper.
d.x: The goal was disallowed because the player was offside.

d.g: To overrule a colonial legislation by the sovereign-in-privy council.

disallow.e: From Middle English disallowen, desallowen, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman desalouer, Old French desalöer. By surface analysis, dis- + allow.

d.g: To remove ambiguities from; to make less ambiguous; to clarify or specify which of multiple possibilities applies – e.g., possible meanings of an ambiguous statement – or to invite or require this.
To distinguish one word or lexical unit (from a different one which has a similar form).
d.x: When necessary, the Greek spelling is disambiguated by an appended phonetic transcription.

disambiguate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₂énts? Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰíder. …

d.g: To vanish.
To go missing; to become a missing person.
d.x: Eighteen years after Jaycee Dugard disappeared in 1991, she was found alive in the summer of 2009.

d.g: To go away; to become lost.
d.x: A turban and loincloth soaked in blood had been found; also a staff. These properties were known to have belonged to a toddy drawer. He had disappeared.

d.g: To make vanish; especially, to abduct or murder for political reasons.
d.x: The Chinese government is well-known for disappearing particularly vocal political dissidents.

disappear.e: From Middle English disapeeren, equivalent to dis- + appear. Displaced native Old English fordwīnan. Displaced native Old English cwincan, whose causative persists as quench (“put out (fire)”).

d.g: To sadden or displease (someone) by underperforming, or by not delivering something promised or hoped for.
d.x: His lack of respect disappointed her.

d.g: To deprive (someone of something expected or hoped for).
d.x: […] you shan’t be disappointed of a wedding—you shall come to mine.

d.g: To fail to meet (an expectation); to fail to fulfil (a hope).
d.x: “But perhaps your accommodations—your cottage—your furniture—have disappointed your expectations?”

d.g: To show (an opinion, belief, etc.) to be mistaken.
d.x: I am sure you will not disappoint my opinion of you, by failing at any time to treat your aunt Norris with the respect and attention that are due to her.

disappoint.e: From Middle French desapointer (compare French désappointer). The word originally meant to "dispossess of appointed office", and eventually broadened to mean "to frustrate the expectations or desires of" and "defeat the realization or fulfillment of".

d.g: To condemn; to consider wrong or inappropriate; used with of.
d.x: She disapproves of rap music because of its sometimes aggressive lyrics.

d.g: To have or express an unfavorable opinion.
d.x: Green washing schemes of corporations are disapproved by Greenpeace activists.

d.g: To refuse to approve; reject.

disapprove.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To deprive of weapons; to deprive of the means of attack or defense; to render defenseless.
To deprive of the means or the disposition to harm; to render harmless or innocuous.
d.x: to disarm a man's wrath

d.g: To lay down arms; to stand down.
To reduce one's own military forces.

disarm.e: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.

d.g: To undo the arrangement of; to disorder; to derange.
d.x: Stay, dear, you will disarrange your curls—let me untie your hat.

disarrange.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- Old French a- Proto-Indo-European *(H)rek-der. …

d.g: To disjoint.
To amputate (a limb) at a joint without cutting the bone.

disarticulate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English articulate English disarticulate From dis- + articulate.

d.g: To take to pieces; to reverse the process of assembly.
d.x: To perform the repair it was necessary to disassemble most of the mechanism.

d.g: To convert machine code to a human-readable, mnemonic form.

disassemble.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To separate (oneself); to dissolve one's association with a person, group, or situation.
d.x: After the scandal, the political party disassociated itself from the questionable candidate.

d.g: To separate into smaller discrete units, as with analysis.
d.x: The problem is easier to understand if you disassociate the variables.

d.g: To separate; to disunite; to disintegrate; to dissolve.
d.x: The fibers of this nonwoven textile disassociated when I tried to wash it.

d.g: Alternative form of dissociate.

disassociate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English associate English disassociate From dis- + associate.

d.g: To strongly and solemnly refuse to own or acknowledge; to deny responsibility for, approbation of, and the like.
d.x: He was charged with embezzlement, but he disavows the crime.

d.g: To deny; to show the contrary of; to deny legitimacy or achievement of any kind.
d.x: Because of her dissatisfaction, she now disavows the merits of socialism.

disavow.e: From dis- + avow, or from Old French desavouer.

d.g: To break up or (cause to) cease to exist; to disperse.
d.x: The president wanted to disband the scandal-plagued agency.

disband.e: Attested since the 1590s, from Middle French desbander (Modern French débander), from des- (English dis-) + bande (English band), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). By surface analysis, dis- + band.

d.g: To expel from the bar, or the legal profession; to deprive (an attorney, barrister, or counselor) of his or her status and privileges as such.
To exclude (a person) from something.
d.x: The friends of Holmes have been criticising the action of the board in disbarring him on the ground that it was too severe […]

disbar.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English bar English disbar From dis- + bar.

d.g: To not believe; to exercise disbelief.
d.x: If you disbelieve such people, then keep disbelieving them for as long as you live or want.

d.g: To actively deny (a statement, opinion or perception).
d.x: He chose to disbelieve the bad news as inconceivable.

d.g: To cease to believe.
d.x: He never "revolted" against Christianity; only, reluctantly and gradually, disbelieved it.

disbelieve.e: Coined circa 1640, from dis- + believe. Compare misbelieve.

d.g: To remove buds from a plant in order to promote growth and health in the remaining buds.
To remove horn-buds from a young calf, lamb or goat kid, to prevent growth of horns.

disbud.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English bud English disbud From dis- + bud.

d.g: To rid of a burden; to free from a load carried; to unload.
d.x: to disburden a pack animal

d.g: To free from a source of mental trouble.
d.x: My meditations […] will, I hope, be more […] calm, being thus disburdened.

disburden.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English burden English disburden From dis- + burden.

d.g: To pay out, expend; usually from a public fund or treasury.

disburse.e: From Old French desbourser (Modern French débourser). By surface analysis, dis- + burse (“purse”).

d.g: get undressed

discase.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English case English discase From dis- + case.

d.g: To detect with the senses, especially with the eyes.
To perceive, recognize, or comprehend with the mind; to descry.
To distinguish something as being different from something else; to differentiate or discriminate.
d.x: He was too young to discern right from wrong.

d.g: To perceive differences.

discern.e: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.

d.g: To tear into pieces; to rend.
To separate; to disunite.
d.x: […] to reascend the place from whence they came, and rejoin that Substance from whence they were discerped […]

discerp.e: From Latin discerpō, from dis- + carpō (“to pluck”).

d.g: To completely renounce claims to; to deny ownership of or responsibility for
d.x: He calls the Gods to witness their offence, / Disclaims the War, asserts his Innocence.

d.g: To deny (e.g. claim); to refuse.
d.x: The payment was irregularly made, if not disclaimed.

d.g: (law) To relinquish or deny having a claim; to disavow another's claim; to decline accepting, as an estate, interest, or office.
To make a caveat or admission.
d.x: I disclaim that there will be a lot of inside humor. If you don't read a.r.s often, or are a newbie, you won't get some of the gags.

disclaim.e: From Middle English disclaimen, from Anglo-Norman disclaimer, from Old French desclamer (French déclamer), des- + clamer.

d.g: To uncover; physically expose to view.
d.x: The shells being broken, […] the stone included in them is thereby disclosed and set at liberty.

d.g: To expose to the knowledge of others; to make known; state openly; reveal (something).
d.x: Her lively looks a sprightly mind disclose.

disclose.e: From Middle English disclosen, from Middle French desclos, from Old French desclore, itself from Vulgar Latin disclaudere, from Latin dis- + claudere (“to close, shut”) or as a variant of discludo, discludere (cf. disclude). By surface analysis, dis- + close.

d.g: To change or lose color.
d.x: Washing light laundry with dark may cause your clothes to discolor.

discolor.e: From Middle English discoloren, discoloren, from Old French descolorer, discolorer, equivalent to dis- + color.

d.g: remove color from
remove color from
British and Canadian standard spelling of discolor.

discolour.e: From Middle English discolouren, discoloren, from Old French discolorer, descolorer, equivalent to dis- + colour.

d.g: remove color from
To throw into a state of confusion; to befuddle or perplex.
d.x: The notes zigzag in his pieces and discombobulate the ear, just as in 12-tone works.

discombobulate.e: 1834 US, fanciful variant of discompose, discomfit, etc., originally discombobricate. The -bob- interfix may come from bobbery, meaning “commotion, noise”.

d.g: To embarrass (someone) greatly; to confuse; to perplex; to disconcert.
d.x: Don't worry. Your joke did not really discomfit me.

d.g: To defeat the plans or hopes of; to frustrate; disconcert.
d.x: In these disguises, Maitland argued, he would certainly avoid recognition, and so discomfit any mischief planned by the enemies of Margaret.

discomfit.e: From Middle English discomfiten, from Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire (“to undo, to destroy”), from des- (“completely”), from Latin dis- + Old French confire (“to make”), from Latin cōnficiō (“to finish up, to destroy”), from com- (“with, together”) + faciō (“to do, to make”). …

d.g: To cause inconvenience to (someone).
To destroy the composure of; to disturb or agitate.
d.x: I am glad I have done being in love with him. I should not like a man who is so soon discomposed by a hot morning.

d.g: To disarrange, or throw into a state of disorder.
d.x:
If e'er with airy horns I planted heads,
Or rumpled petticoats, or tumbled beds,
Or caus'd suspicion when no soul was rude,

discompose.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English compose English discompose From dis- + compose.

d.g: To upset the composure of; to startle.
d.x: The embrace disconcerted the daughter-in-law somewhat, as the caresses of old gentlemen unshorn and perfumed with tobacco might well do.

d.g: To bring into confusion.
To frustrate, discomfit.
d.x: The emperor disconcerted the plans of his enemy.

d.g: A state of disunion.

disconcert.e: From Middle French desconcerter, from des- (“dis-”) + concerter (“to bring into agreement, organize”).

d.g: To interrupt the continuance of; to put an end to, especially as regards commercial productions; to stop producing, making, or supplying.
d.x: They plan to discontinue that design.

d.g: To consciously cease the ingestion or administration of (a pharmaceutical drug).

discontinue.e: From Old French descontinuer, equivalent to dis- + continue.

d.g: To have an unfavorable opinion of; to deprecate or disapprove of.
d.x: A town meeting was convened to discountenance riot.

d.g: To abash, embarrass or disconcert.
d.x: The hermit was somewhat discountenanced by this observation.

d.g: To refuse countenance or support to; to discourage.
d.x: These were rejected by Parliament, which discountenanced the amalgamation of competing lines but gave broad approval in theory to end-on amalgamations.

d.g: Cold treatment; disapprobation.

discountenance.e: From Middle French descontenancer (compare French décontenancer).

d.g: To extinguish the courage of; to dishearten; to depress the spirits of; to deprive of confidence; to deject.
d.x: Don't be discouraged by the amount of work left to do: you'll finish it in good time.

d.g: To persuade somebody not to do (something).
d.x: Discourage litigation. Persuade your neighbors to compromise whenever you can.

d.g: Lack of courage

discourage.e: From Middle French descourager (modern French décourager), from Old French descouragier, from des- and corage. By surface analysis, dis- + courage.

d.g: To find or learn something for the first time.
d.x: Turning the corner, I discovered a lovely little shop. I discovered that they sold widgets.

d.g: To create by moving a piece out of another piece's line of attack.
d.x: This move discovers an attack on a vital pawn.

d.g: To question (a person) as part of discovery in a lawsuit.

discover.e: From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Displaced native Old English onfindan.

d.g: To converse or debate concerning a particular topic.
d.x: Let's sit down and discuss whether we should have a baby.

d.g: To examine or search thoroughly; to exhaust a remedy against, as against a principal debtor before proceeding against the surety.
To deal with, in eating or drinking; consume.
d.x: When the preparations were finished, he invited me with—“Now, sir, bring forward your chair.” And we all, including the rustic youth, drew round the table: an austere silence prevailing while we discussed our meal.

discuss.e: From Middle English discussen, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman discusser (French discuter), from Latin discussus, past participle of discutiō (“to strike or shake apart, break up, scatter; examine, discuss”), from dis- (“apart”) + quatiō (“to shake”).

d.g: To remove from on board a vessel; to put on shore
d.x: The general disembarked the troops.

d.g: To go ashore from a ship, boat, train, or aircraft; to leave.
d.x: We disembarked the ferry.

disembark.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English em- English bark English embark English disembark From dis- + embark.

d.g: To get (someone) out of a difficult or embarrassing situation; to free (someone) from the embarrassment (of a situation); (often reflexive) to relieve (someone of a burden, item of clothing, etc.).
d.x: He had now disembarrassed himself of his riding-dress, and walking up to his daughter, he undid the fastening of her mask.

disembarrass.e: From dis- + embarrass. Possibly a calque of French désembarrasser. First attested in 1726 (sense 1).

d.g: To cause someone's soul, spirit, consciousness, voice, etc, to become separated from the physical body.
To separate (a part of the body) from the body.
d.x: Jerusha turned, a flush on her cheeks that wasn't makeup, a swath of steam from the vaporizer swirling around her chest, disembodying her head.

d.g: To discharge from military service or array.

disembody.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English embody English disembody From dis- + embody.

d.g: To take or let out the bowels or interior parts of; to eviscerate.
To take or draw from the body, as the web of a spider.

disembowel.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English embowel English disembowel From dis- + embowel.

d.g: To free or extricate from confusion
To disable (render unable)
d.x: The sight of it might damp me and disenable me to speak.

d.g: To free from illusion, false belief or enchantment; to undeceive or disillusion.
To disappoint.
To break from a mental captivation such as reverie (daydream) or preoccupation.
To remove a spell or magic enchantment from.

disenchant.e: From Middle French desenchanter, equivalent to dis- + enchant.

d.g: To remove an encumbrance or burden from (someone or something); unburden.
d.x: Francesca was soon disencumbered of her riding-hood and cloak; and the three young people, left together, became rapidly acquainted.

disencumber.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English encumber English disencumber From dis- + encumber.

d.g: To deprive someone of a franchise, generally of the right to vote.
A circular movement of the blade that avoids the opponent's parry
To release or loosen from something that binds, entangles, holds, or interlocks.
d.x: The more established wisdom about trolls, at this point, is to disengage.

disengage.e: From Middle French désengager ; dis- + engage.

d.g: To free something from entanglement; to extricate or unknot.
d.x: I had to disentangle him from his own shoelaces.

d.g: To unravel; to separate into discrete components or units.
d.x: This overlapping is reflective of hybrid languages, where certain features (phonetic, orthographic, semantic, syntactic) are also difficult to disentangle.

d.g: To become free or untangled.

disentangle.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Middle English entanglen English entangle English disentangle From dis- + entangle.

d.g: To deprive (an established church, military squadron, operations base, etc.) of its official status.
d.x: Furthermore, disestablishing the Catholic church in February 1795 essentially instituted a free field in religious belief.

d.g: To abolish (an existing position of employment).

disestablish.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English establish English disestablish From dis- + establish.

d.g: to irreversibly damage the shape or structure of something, negatively affecting its appearance or functionality without completely destroying it.
d.x: His face was disfigured by a terrible fire many years ago, leaving deep scars across his crooked nose.

disfigure.e: From Middle English disfiguren, from Anglo-Norman desfigurer.

d.g: To disafforest
To deprive someone of some privilege, especially the right to vote; to disenfranchise.
d.x: Jewish culture, the product of a small, oppressed, and disfranchised dwindling and scattered minority.

disfranchise.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English franchise English disfranchise From dis- + franchise.

d.g: To vomit or spew, to discharge.
d.x: They loudly laughed / To see his heaving breast disgorge the briny draught.

d.g: To surrender (stolen goods or money, for example) unwillingly.
To remove traces of yeast from sparkling wine by the méthode champenoise.
To make discontent or cross; to put in a bad temper.
d.x: A pregnant woman who ordered pizza in Florida was stabbed 14 times by a delivery driver who police say was disgruntled over her $2 tip.

disgruntle.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English gruntle English disgruntle From dis- (intensifier) + gruntle (“grumble, grunt”).

d.g: To create or introduce disorder.
To discourage someone by removing their enthusiasm or courage.
d.x: The repeated failures began to dishearten the team.

dishearten.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To throw into disorder; upheave.
d.x: The wind disheveled the papers on the desk.

d.g: To disarrange or loosen (hair, clothing, etc.).
d.x: With garments rent, and haire discheueled, / Wringing her hands, and making piteous mone;

d.g: To spread out in disorder.

dishevel.e: From Old French descheveler (modern French écheveler, ultimately from Old French chevel).

d.g: lacking a physical form.
To divest of body; to make immaterial.
To die, in context of subsequently existing outside the body (for example, as a soul or spirit).

disincarnate.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English incarnate English disincarnate From dis- + incarnate.

d.g: To make reluctant; to lessen the inclination of.

disincline.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Latin inclīnāre Old French enclinerbor. Middle English enclinen English incline English disincline From dis- + incline.

d.g: To sterilize by the use of cleaning agent.
d.x: An on-board cleaner passes through, disinfecting every grabrail and handhold as they pass.

disinfect.e: From English dis- + infect, from Middle French desinfecter.

d.g: To eliminate insects, vermin, or other pests from.

disinfest.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English infest English disinfest From dis- + infest.

d.g: To exclude from inheritance; to disown.
d.x: Excuses for disinheriting people, that we swear we're not making up

disinherit.e: From Middle English disenheriten, equivalent to dis- + inherit.

d.g: To undo the integrity of; to break into parts.
d.x: Marlites […] are not disintegrated by exposure to the atmosphere, at least in six years.

d.g: To cause to break up into infinitesimal parts through the use of a disintegrator.
To fall apart; to break up into parts.
d.x: Hence they are eloquent, not of the present, disintegrating society and psyche, but of the unquenched source through which society is reborn.

d.g: To take out of the grave or tomb.
To bring out, as from a grave or hiding place; to bring from obscurity into view.
d.x: Why disinter dead faith from mouldering hidden?

disinter.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des- Middle French des- French dés- French enterrer French désenterrerbor. English disinter Borrowed from French désenterrer.

d.g: To reduce investment, or cease to invest.

disinvest.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To uncover; to unfold or unroll; to disentangle.
d.x: And for that second sense, it is indeed disinvolved of those former Difficulties

d.g: To terminate the involvement of.
d.x: Has the author processed his subject in such a way as to exclude, to pacify, to disinvolve the reader?

d.g: To separate; to disunite.
d.x: That marriage, therefore, God himself disjoins.

d.g: To become separated.

disjoin.e: From Middle English disjoynen, from Old French desjoindre, from Latin disiungere (“to separate”), from dis-, di- (“apart”) + iungere (“to join”). Equivalent to dis- + join.

d.g: To put something out of its usual place.
To emotionally jar, unsettle, or disorient.
To (accidentally) dislodge a skeletal bone from its joint.

dislocate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English locate English dislocate From dis- + locate.

d.g: To remove or force out from a position or dwelling previously occupied.
d.x: In 1955, No. 30783, after a collision with an H15 4-6-0 at Bournemouth in which its right-hand cylinder was dislodged, required very extensive frame renewals.

d.g: To move or go from a dwelling or former position.
d.x: Where Light and Darkness in perpetual round / Lodge and dislodge by turns.

d.g: To force out of a secure or settled position.

dislodge.e: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Compare French déloger. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.

d.g: To take apart; to disassemble; to take to pieces.
To disprove a discourse, claim or argument.
d.x: If we can dismantle hate rhetoric and explain why it is, in fact, illogical, is the language no longer dangerous?

d.g: To divest, strip of dress or covering.
To remove fittings or furnishings from.

dismantle.e: From Middle French desmanteler, itself from des- (“dis-”), mantel (“coat”) + -er (verbal suffix). Compare typologically uncloak, reveal, unmask.

d.g: To remove the limbs of.
d.x: Death by drawing and quartering usually dismembered the condemned person.

d.g: To cut or otherwise divide something into pieces.
d.x: The killer methodically dismembered the bodies of his victims.

dismember.e: From Middle English, from Old French desmembrer, from des- (“de-”) + membre (“limb”) + -er (“verbal suffix”).

d.g: To discharge; to end the employment or service of.
d.x: The company dismissed me after less than a year.

d.g: To order to leave.
d.x: The soldiers were dismissed after the parade.

d.g: To dispel; to rid one’s mind of.
d.x: He dismissed all thoughts of acting again.

d.g: To reject; to refuse to accept.
d.x: The court dismissed the case.

d.g: To invalidate; to treat as unworthy of serious consideration.
d.x: By telling the victim to "get over it", the listener dismissed the victim's feelings.

d.g: To send or put away, to discard with disregard, contempt or disdain. (sometimes followed by as).
d.x: She dismissed him with a wave of the hand.

d.g: To get a batsman out.
d.x: He was dismissed for 99 runs.

d.g: To give someone a red card; to send off.
d.x: Kalinic later saw red for a rash tackle on Paul Scharner before Gabriel Tamas was dismissed for bringing down Diouf.

d.g: bar from attention or consideration

dismiss.e: Middle English, from Latin dimissus (“sent away, dismissed, banished”), perfect passive participle of dīmittō (“send away, dismiss”), from dis- + mittere (“to send”).

d.g: To refuse or intentionally fail to obey.
d.x: disobey the rules

d.g: to be unwilling to oblige; to disappoint, to inconvenience, not to cooperate.
d.x: Sorry to disoblige everybody; I know you were depending on me to bring a good weather forecast for our fête, but it is going to rain.

d.g: To offend by an act of unkindness or incivility.

disoblige.e: From Middle French desobliger. By surface analysis, dis- + oblige.

d.g: To make less organised; to reduce to chaos.
d.x: The arrival of her new baby would inevitably disorganise her life.

d.g: To make less organized; to reduce to chaos.
d.x: The arrival of her new baby would inevitably disorganize her life.

disorganize.e: From French désorganiser, equivalent to dis- + organize.

d.g: To cause to lose orientation or direction.
To confuse or befuddle.

disorient.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des- Middle French des- French dés- French orienter French désorienterbor. English disorient Borrowed from French désorienter.

d.g: Alternative form of disorient.

disorientate.e: From dis- + orientate. Not a back-formation from disorientation, which is attested much later and is perhaps from disorientate.

d.g: To refuse to own, or to refuse to acknowledge one’s own.
d.x: Lord Capulet and his wife threatened to disown their daughter Juliet if she didn’t go through with marrying Count Paris.

d.g: To repudiate any connection to; to renounce.
d.x: He disowns me, and he scorns me / But when we're alone he tells me I'm his very own

d.g: To detach (a job or process) so that it can continue to run even when the user who launched it ends his/her login session.

disown.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English own English disown From dis- + own.

d.g: To dishonor by a comparison with what is inferior; to lower in rank or estimation by actions or words; to speak slightingly of; to depreciate; to undervalue.
d.x: Thou durst not thus disparage glorious arms.

d.g: To ridicule, mock, discredit.
d.x: Had he disparaged my personal appearance I should in all probability have laughed at him with lively indifference

disparage.e: From Middle English disparage (noun), disparagen (verb), from Old French desparage (noun), desparagier (verb), from des- (“dis-”) + parage (“equal rank, rank”).

d.g: To drive away or cause to vanish by scattering.
d.x: The clouds and mist were soon enough dispelled by the sun.

d.g: To remove (fears, doubts, objections etc.) by proving them unjustified.
To get rid of or manage without.
An act or instance of dispelling.
d.x: “My dispel didn't work,” she said finally. “He wasn't a blood witch, Sunny,” I said.

dispel.e: From Middle English dispelen, from Latin dispellere (“to disperse; to dispel”).

d.g: To issue, distribute, or give out.
d.x: He is delighted to dispense a share of it to all the company.

d.g: To apply, as laws to particular cases; to administer; to execute; to manage; to direct.
d.x: to dispense justice

d.g: To supply or make up a medicine or prescription.
d.x: The pharmacist dispensed my tablets.

d.g: To give a dispensation to (someone); to excuse.
d.x: After his victories, he often gave them the reines to all licenciousnesse, for a while dispencing them from all rules of military discipline[…].

dispense.e: From Middle English, from Old French dispenser, from Latin dispēnsāre (“to weigh out, pay out, distribute, regulate, manage, control, dispense”), frequentative of dispendere (“to weigh out”), from dis- (“apart”) + pendere (“to weigh”).

d.g: To scatter in different directions.
d.x: The Jews are dispersed among all nations.

d.g: To break up and disappear; to dissipate.
To disseminate.
To separate rays of light, etc., according to wavelength; to refract.

disperse.e: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

d.g: To lower the morale of; to make despondent; to dishearten.

dispirit.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys-der.? Latin spīrō Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus Latin spīritus Old French espiritbor. …

d.g: To put out of place; to disarrange.
To move something, or someone, especially to forcibly move people from their homeland.
d.x: Manipur: Thousands displaced as ethnic clashes grip north-eastern state

d.g: To supplant, or take the place of something or someone; to substitute.
To replace, on account of being superior to or more suitable than that which is being replaced.
d.x: Electronic calculators soon displaced the older mechanical kind.

d.g: To make not pleased; to cause a feeling of disapprobation or dislike in; to be disagreeable to; to vex slightly.
d.x: The boy's rudeness displeased me.

d.g: To give displeasure or offense.

displease.e: English dis- + please, from Middle English displesen, from Anglo-Norman despleisir, desplere, from Old French desplere (des- + plere).

d.g: To deprive of feathers or plumes.
To strip of an award.

displume.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English plume English displume From dis- + plume.

d.g: To amuse oneself divertingly or playfully; in particular, to cavort or gambol.
d.x: What generous, ardent, imaginative soul has not a secret pleasure-place in which it disports?

disport.e: The verb is derived from Middle English disporten, desporten (“to take part in entertainment, sport, etc., to pass time, amuse oneself, be merry; to amuse, entertain; to cheer, console; to behave (in a particular way), deport; to be active, to busy; to relieve (someone of a task); to prevent (someone from attending)”), …

d.g: To eliminate or to get rid of something.
d.x: I dispose of my trash in the garbage can.

d.g: To distribute or arrange; to put in place.
d.x: Now, dear soldiers, march away: / And how thou pleasest, God, dispose the day!

d.g: To deal out; to assign to a use.
d.x: what he designed to bestow on her funeral, he would rather dispose among the poor

d.g: To incline.
d.x: In these uncertain times, I am disposed towards caution.

d.g: give, sell, or transfer to another

dispose.e: French disposerbor. English dispose Borrowed from French disposer.

d.g: To deprive someone of the possession of land, especially by evicting them.
To deprive someone of possession in general.
To take possession of the ball/puck etc. (from someone).
d.x: It was Bannan who released Agbonlahor for his goal with a long-range curling pass after Stephen Warnock had dispossessed Mohamed Diame.

dispossess.e: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French despossesser. Equivalent to dis- + possess.

d.g: spread abroad or out
To spread out, to extend.
d.x: In widest Ocean she her throne does reare, / That ouer all the earth it may be seene; / As morning Sunne her beames dispredden cleare [...].

d.g: To prove to be false or erroneous; to confute; to refute.
d.x: disprove a theory

disprove.e: From Middle English disproven, dispreven, from Old French desprover, from des- + prover, equivalent to dis- + prove.

d.g: To make ineligible for something.
d.x: My age disqualifies me for the position.

d.g: To exclude from consideration by the explicit revocation of a previous qualification.
d.x: The athlete was disqualified after performance-enhancing drugs were found in his hotel room.

disqualify.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English qualify English disqualify From dis- + qualify.

d.g: To uncover clothing by removing it oneself or someone else.
d.x: Goddamn this claustrophobia / 'Cause I should be disrobin’ ya

disrobe.e: From dis- + robe. Compare Old French desrober in the same sense.

d.g: To throw into confusion or disorder.
d.x: Hecklers disrupted the man's speech.

d.g: To interrupt or impede.
d.x: Work on the tunnel was disrupted by a strike.

d.g: To improve a product or service in ways that displace an established one and surprise the market.
d.x: The internet makes it easier for leaner businesses to disrupt the larger and more unwieldy ones.

disrupt.e: Borrowed from Latin disruptus, from disrumpo, commonly dirumpo (“to break or burst asunder”), from dis-, di- (“apart, asunder”) + rumpo (“to break”).

d.g: To put (someone) down, or show disrespect by the use of insulting language or dismissive behaviour.
An insult or put-down; an expression of disrespect.
Dissertation.
d.x: I've been wondering what happens if I fail my diss. I know i'm allowed to fail 60 credits but I don't think that includes the diss.

d.g: Ampelodesmos mauritanicus syn. Ampelodesmos tenax, a reedy grass used for cordage.

diss.e: Originated in Jamaican English or African American Vernacular English, probably originally a clipping of disrespect or disparage, both from the prefix dis-, ultimately from Latin dis-.

d.g: To fail to satisfy; to displease.

dissatisfy.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English satisfy English dissatisfy From dis- + satisfy.

d.g: To study an animal's anatomy by cutting it apart; to perform a necropsy or an autopsy.
d.x: She was the first person in her class to properly dissect the sheep heart.

d.g: To study a plant's or other organism's anatomy similarly.
To analyze an idea in detail by delineating between its parts.
To decontextualize an idea, especially through overanalysis by delineating between its parts too strongly based on style, usually involving pedantry, at the expense of substance.
d.x: Academics tend to take Indigenous oral histories out of their contexts and dissect them according to Western disciplinary objectives and foci (see figure 1).

dissect.e: Borrowed from Latin dissectus past participle of dissecare (“to cut asunder, cut up”), from dis- (“asunder”) + secare (“to cut”); see section.

d.g: To disguise or conceal something.
d.x: Dissemble all your griefs and discontents.

d.g: To feign, dissimulate.
d.x: And like a Lyon, Slumbring in the vvay, / Or Sleep-diſſembling, vvhile he vvaits his Prey, […]

d.g: To deliberately ignore something; to pretend not to notice.
To falsely hide one's opinions or feelings.

dissemble.e: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dissemblen, dissimblen, dissemelen, borrowed from Old French dessambler, dissembler, disembler, itself borrowed from Latin dissimulō and modified after sembler, semblance, etc. …

d.g: To sow and scatter principles, ideas, opinions, etc, or concrete things, for growth and propagation, like seeds.
To become widespread.
d.x: The values of the human rights movement have disseminated throughout the world.

disseminate.e: Borrowed from Latin dissēminātus, the perfect passive participle of dissēminō (“to broadcast, disseminate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from dis- (“asunder, in all directions”) + sēminō (“to plant, sow”), from sēmen (“seed”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). …

d.g: To make a dissertation; to discourse.
To write one's dissertation.
d.x: Mark stayed up until 2 a.m. dissertating last night.

dissertate.e: First attested in 1766; borrowed from Latin dissertātus, perfect passive participle of dissertō (“to argue, discuss”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of disserō. Doublet of dissert.

d.g: To divide and separate something into separate parts.
d.x: [T]he ſaid floud of Rubicon diſſeuereth the Galle Ciſalpine from Italie.

dissever.e: From Middle English disseveren, from Anglo-Norman desevrer, Old French dessevrer, from Vulgar Latin *dissēperō, dissēperāre, from Latin dis- + sēparō.

d.g: To change and become different from what was originally similar.

dissimilate.e: First attested in 1841; borrowed from Medieval Latin dissimilātus, perfect passive participle of dissimilō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), hypercorrected form of Classical Latin dissimulō, from dis- + simulō, from similis (“similar, the same as”); the vocalism was perhaps influenced by assimilate, compare dissimulate …

d.g: To disguise or conceal one's true feelings, motives, or identity by adopting a false appearance.
d.x: [P]ublic feeling required the meagreness of nature to be dissimulated by tall barricades of frizzed curls and bows.

d.g: To connive at; to wink at; to pretend not to notice.

dissimulate.e: Inherited from Middle English dissimulaten, dissimilaten, from Latin dissimulātus + -en (“verb-forming suffix”), perfect passive participle of dissimulō (“to conceal, to pretend, to neglect”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dissimilis (“unlike”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). …

d.g: To drive away, disperse.
d.x:
August 1773, James Cook, journal entry
I soon dissipated his fears.

d.g: To use up or waste; squander.
d.x: The vast wealth […] was in three years dissipated.

d.g: To vanish by dispersion.
To cause energy to be lost through its conversion to heat.
To be dissolute in conduct.

dissipate.e: The verb is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765; from Middle English dissipaten, from Latin dissipātus, perfect passive participle of dissipō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), also written dissupō (“to scatter, disperse, demolish, destroy, squan …

d.g: To make unrelated; to sever a connection; to separate.
d.x: A number of group members wish to dissociate themselves from the majority.

d.g: To part; to stop associating.
d.x: After the big fight, the gang totally dissociated from each other.

d.g: To separate compounds into simpler component parts, usually by applying heat or through electrolysis.
d.x: We dissociated the lead iodide into its elements by heating

d.g: To undergo dissociation.

dissociate.e: From Latin dissociō (“dissociate”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from dis- (“apart”) + sociō (“join”), from socius (“related, leagued”).

d.g: To be dissonant.
To cause dissonance (in all senses).
To convince not to try or do.
d.x: Jane dissuaded Martha from committing suicide.

dissuade.e: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

d.g: To extend or expand, as from internal pressure; to swell
d.x: I begin to hate the theater, the feeling wickedly distended by histrionics, all the old gestures, clutchings, tears, and applications.

d.g: To cause to swell.
To cause gravidity.
become wider

distend.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Proto-Indo-European *ten- Proto-Indo-European *tend-der. Proto-Italic *tendō Latin tendō Latin distendōbor. English distend Borrowed from Latin distendō.

d.g: To exude (a liquid) in small drops; also, to give off (a vapour) which condenses in small drops.
d.x: Firs distil resin.

d.g: To impart (information, etc.) in small quantities; to infuse.
d.x:
She felt the slackening frost distil
 Through her blood the last ooze dull and chill:
 Her lids were dry and her lips were still.

d.g: To heat (a substance, usually a liquid) so that a vapour is produced, and then to cool the vapour so that it condenses back into a liquid, either to purify the original substance or to obtain one of its components; to subject to distillation.
d.x:
Haue I not bene
 Thy Pupill long? Haſt thou not learn'd me how
 To make Perfumes? Diſtill? Preſerue?

d.g: Followed by off or out: to expel (a volatile substance) from something by distillation.

distil.e: From Late Middle English distillen (“to fall, flow, or shed in drops, drop, trickle; to shed drops; to fill (the eyes) with tears; (alchemy, medicine) to subject (something) to distillation; to obtain (something) using distillation; to distil; to condense or vaporize; (figuratively) to give (good fortune) to; to say (s …

d.g: US standard spelling of distil.
d.x: There is ſome ſoule of goodneſſe in things euill, / VVould men obſeruingly diſtill it out.

d.g: To recognize someone or something as different from others based on its characteristics.
To see someone or something clearly or distinctly.
To make noticeably different or better from others through accomplishments.
d.x: The soldier distinguished himself in combat and received a medal.

d.g: To confer an honor upon.
d.x: The soldier was distinguished with a medal for his bravery.

distinguish.e: From Middle English distingwen, from Old French distinguer, from Latin distinguere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from di-, dis- (“apart”) + stinguere, related to English stink. Compare extinguish.

d.g: To bring something out of shape, to misshape.
To become misshapen.
To give a false or misleading account of; pervert.
d.x: In their articles, journalists sometimes distort the truth.

distort.e: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).

d.g: To divert attention.
d.x: The crowd was distracted by a helicopter hovering over the stadium when the only goal of the game was scored.

d.g: To make crazy or insane; to drive to distraction.
d.x:
By Heav’ns, ſuch Virtues, join’d with ſuch Succeſs,
Diſtract my very Soul: Our Father’s Fortune
Wou’d almoſt tempt us to renounce his Precepts.

distract.e: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).

d.g: To seize somebody's property in place of, or to force, payment of a debt.

distrain.e: From Middle English distreynen, from Old French destraindre, from Latin distringō (“to pull asunder”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringō (“to draw tight, strain”).

d.g: To divide into portions and dispense.
d.x: He distributed the bread amongst his followers.

d.g: To supply to retail outlets.
d.x: The agency distributes newspapers to local shops.

d.g: To deliver or pass out.
d.x: A network of children distributes flyers to every house.

d.g: To scatter or spread.
d.x: I raked the soil then distributed grass seed.

d.g: To employ (a term) in its whole extent; to take as universal in one premise.
d.x: A term is said to be distributed when it is taken universal, so as to stand for everything it is capable of being applied to.

distribute.e: PIE word *tréyes From Latin distributus, past participle of distribuere (“to divide, distribute”), from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to give, impart”); see tribute.

d.g: to confuse a quiet, constant state or a calm, continuous flow, in particular: thoughts, actions or liquids.
d.x: The noisy ventilation disturbed me during the exam.

d.g: to divert, redirect, or alter by disturbing.
d.x: A mudslide disturbed the course of the river.

d.g: to have a negative emotional impact; to cause emotional distress or confusion.

disturb.e: From Middle English destourben, from Anglo-Norman distourber and Old French destorber, from Latin disturbare, intensifying for turbare (“to throw into disorder”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH-, *(s)turH- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).

d.g: To cause to cease to be unified; to split up or dissociate.
To cause disagreement or alienation among or within.
d.x: If they cannot disunite them by domestic broils, then they engage their neighbours against them.

d.g: To separate, sever, or split.
d.x: I have discovered how to disunite that force and that particle.

d.g: To disintegrate; to come apart.
d.x:
You cannot bind me more to you, my lord.
Farewell till we renew... I trust, renew
A converse ne'er to disunite again.

disunite.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *ís? Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos Proto-Italic *oinos Old Latin oinos Latin ūnus Proto-Indo-European *-yétider. …

d.g: To wander about.
To stray from a subject or theme.
d.x: The fallen guillotine blade is replaced with a call to awareness that, as we have seen, divagates from Szpiner's "Ayez pitié des enfants."

divagate.e: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin dīvagātus, perfect active participle of dīvagor (“to wander here and there”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dis- (“in different direction”) + vagor (“to wander”). Cognate with French divaguer.

d.g: To spread apart; to (cause to) diverge or branch off.
Having wide angles between the branches.

divaricate.e: The verb is first attested in 1623, the adjective in 1788; borrowed from Latin dīvāricātus, perfect passive participle of dīvāricō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dis- + vāricō (“to straddle, to stretch (the legs) apart”), from vāricus (“straddling”).

d.g: To become different and run apart; to separate and tend towards different directions.
d.x: Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, / And sorry I could not travel both / […]

d.g: To separate, to tend into a different direction (from another line or path).
d.x: The sidewalk runs next to the street for a few miles, then diverges from it and turns north.

diverge.e: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

d.g: To make (something) diverse or varied in form or quality; to give variety to (something) to distinguish by numerous aspects or differences.
To make the scope of (business, investments, etc.) diverse, especially so as to balance and mitigate risks.

diversify.e: Borrowed from Middle French diversifier, equivalent to diverse + -ify.

ori.gloss: vertex, vertical, vertigo, evert, invert — physical rotation or turning in space; orientation

origin.label: Rotational & spatial turning
origin.gloss: vertex, vertical, vertigo, evert, invert — physical rotation or turning in space; orientation

d.g: To turn aside from a course.
d.x: The workers diverted the stream away from the road.

d.g: To distract.
d.x: Don't let him divert your attention; keep your eye on the ball.

d.g: To entertain or amuse (by diverting the attention)
d.x: We are amused by a tale, diverted by a comedy.

d.g: turn aside;  turn away from

divert.e: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

ori.gloss: vertex, vertical, vertigo, evert, invert — physical rotation or turning in space; orientation

origin.label: Rotational & spatial turning
origin.gloss: vertex, vertical, vertigo, evert, invert — physical rotation or turning in space; orientation

d.g: To strip, deprive, or dispossess (someone) of something (such as a right, passion, privilege, or prejudice).
d.x: You shall never divest me of my right to free speech.

d.g: To sell off or be rid of through sale, especially of a subsidiary.
d.x: In 2011, the company divested an 81% majority stake in its foreign subsidiary.

divest.e: Alteration of devest, from Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

d.g: To make public or known; to communicate to the public; to tell (information, especially a secret) so that it may become generally known.
d.x: I will never divulge that secret to anyone.

d.g: To indicate publicly; to proclaim.
d.x: God... marks The just man, and divulges him through heaven.

divulge.e: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).

d.g: To dress with flax for spinning.
To dress with clothes; attire; deck; bedizen.
d.x: Like a tragedy queen he has dizen'd her out, / Or rather like tragedy giving a rout.

d.g: To dress showily; adorn; dress out.

dizen.e: From dialectal dize (“to put tow on a distaff”), from Middle English *disen, from Old English *disan, *disian, from *dise, *disen (“bunch of flax on a distaff”), from Proto-Germanic *disanō (“distaff”), of unknown origin, equivalent to dize + -en. …

d.g: The noun or noun phrase that a verb is directly acting upon.
Such an object when it is in the accusative case, but (generally) not when it is in another case.
A gadget, device, or object whose name is either unknown, forgotten, or omitted for the purpose of humor.
d.x: "If anybody should come in, and catch you with your breeches, as it were, down on the floor, all you have to do is to drink the water, wrap the rubber dingus around you, and tell them to “lay on Macduff.”

d.g: A foolish, incompetent, or silly person.
d.x: I just lost my keys again. Now I feel like a dingus.

d.g: The penis.
d.x: "He got mad at me because his dingus wouldn’t come up for him — too drunk, I guess. […]

dingus.e: Probably of multiple origins. Partly a borrowing from Dutch dinges (“thingamajig, thingy; whatshisname, whatshername”), ding (“thing”). [references] The primary measure of defect damages is the cost of either correcting the defect or supplying the omission. This is known as the cost-of-correction rule. [references] This measure will be applied even though it may cost somewhat more to correct the defects than to have constructed the improvement to real property properly in the first place. Nevertheless the diminished value rule will be applied instead if correcting the defect or supplying the omission involves unreasonable economic waste because the cost of correction is materially disproportionate to the increased value that it would produce. The recovery for diminished value is the difference between the value the improvement would have had if properly constructed and the value as actually constructed. If, after construction defects have been corrected, the building still does not have the value it would have had if it had been constructed properly, the property owner may be able to recover both the cost-of-correction and the remaining diminished value.
